subject: math

unit.title: Statistics, shape and symmetry
unit.essentialQuestion: How do we record data, and how do we describe shapes by their parts and their symmetry?

title: Retrieval & fluency: shape, data and symmetry
objectives: By the end, I can quickly recall shape properties, read a chart and spot symmetry.

vocabulary.definition: the little note on a pictogram that says what ONE symbol is worth
a straight edge of a flat shape
a corner where two sides meet (more than one: vertices)
a flat surface of a solid shape
where two faces of a solid meet
a fold line where both halves match exactly
vocabulary.example: a square has 4 lines of symmetry

emphasize: This is a fluency workout — fast, accurate recall of Unit 7, NO new idea.
Charts → read the KEY first; solids → count the HIDDEN parts too.
Mix the question types so the child has to choose the right approach each time.

misconceptions: reading a keyed pictogram as one-each (ignoring the key)
mixing 2-D and 3-D words (saying 'faces' for a flat shape)
counting only the faces you can see — 'a cube has 4 faces'
assuming any line through a shape is a line of symmetry
hooks: Quiz challenge — how many can you fire back without a pause?

digital: quiz blocks with charts and shape pictures
streak counter framing in the script

plan.goal: Set up the quiz-challenge energy and retrieve an easy shape fact to start the streak.
plan.note: Light, fast rhythm from the first second. Warm-up question must be a guaranteed win.
plan.successCriteria: Child answers 'a triangle has 3 sides' quickly and wants more questions.

script.say: Quiz challenge! Today there's nothing new to learn — just everything from our shape and chart unit, fired at you fast. How many can you answer without a pause? Let's warm up nice and easy: a triangle — how many sides?
script.adaptHints: Match the child's energy; frame the streak like their favourite game (levels, points, a high score to beat).

blocks.caption: Shapes, charts and symmetry — quick-fire round!

stuckProtocol: If even the triangle is shaky: draw a triangle and count its sides together — 1, 2, 3 — then re-ask. Start the streak at one.

plan.goal: Model the answering routine: charts → key first; solids → count the hidden parts in your mind.
plan.note: Short warm-up teach, not a full explain — just the two habits that catch most mistakes.
plan.successCriteria: Child can say the two rules back: 'key first' and 'count the hidden ones too'.

script.say: Watch how a quiz champion answers. Rule one: if it's a chart, read the KEY first. Look — this pictogram's key says one apple picture is worth 2. Three apple pictures: 2, 4, 6. Not three — six! Rule two: if it's a solid shape, turn it in your mind and count the hidden parts too. A cube: I see 3 faces, but spinning it round in my head… there are 6. Say my two rules back to me?
script.adaptHints: If the child parrots quickly, celebrate and speed up; if not, repeat each rule with the picture once more.

elements.value: Charts → key first · Solids → hidden parts too

plan.goal: Shared round: pentagon sides and vertices, then read 'most' from a quick bar chart.
plan.note: 'We do' — the character asks, the child answers, the character thinks aloud on any wobble.
plan.successCriteria: Child says 5 sides and 5 vertices, and picks the tallest bar for 'most'.

script.say: Practice round together. A pentagon — how many sides, and how many vertices? … Five and five, the corners match the sides! Now a chart one. Here's a block diagram of pets: look at the bars. Which pet is the MOST popular? Remember — the tallest bar wins.
script.adaptHints: If the child hesitates on 'vertices', whisper 'corners'. Swap the pet categories for animals the child loves — keep the numbers.

check.question: Which pet is the most popular on the chart?

wrongAnswers.why: picked 'least' — mixed up most and least
wrongAnswers.remedy: Most means the TALLEST bar. Run your eyes along the tops — which bar reaches highest?

wrongAnswers.why: read the first bar instead of comparing heights
wrongAnswers.remedy: Don't stop at the first bar — compare all three tops. Which is tallest?

plan.goal: Diagnostic: pentagon sides AND vertices — reveals 2-D/3-D word mix-ups and miscounts.
plan.note: After a correct answer, always probe: 'Are sides and vertices always the same number for flat shapes like these?'
plan.successCriteria: Child answers 5 sides, 5 vertices and uses the right words for a flat shape.

script.say: Streak check! A pentagon — tell me its sides AND its vertices. Take a breath, picture it, fire away.
script.adaptHints: If correct and fast, add the probe question; if correct but slow, praise the accuracy and note speed comes with practice.

blocks.explain: A pentagon is a flat shape with 5 straight sides, and 5 vertices where the sides meet.

check.question: How many sides and vertices does a pentagon have?

wrongAnswers.why: mixed 2-D and 3-D words — faces and edges belong to solids
wrongAnswers.remedy: A pentagon is FLAT. Flat shapes have sides and corners — what do we call the corners?

wrongAnswers.why: miscounted or confused it with a square/hexagon
wrongAnswers.remedy: Trace the pentagon with your finger and count each side out loud — 1, 2, 3…

plan.goal: Quick-fire mixed set: shape facts, keyed pictograms, block diagrams, symmetry — keep a visible streak.
plan.note: Director draws from the practiceBank, start level 2, MIX the skills — never two of the same type in a row. Count the streak out loud. Once secure, ask 'explain WHY' on one answer (stretch).
plan.successCriteria: Child answers 4+ mixed items correctly, including a keyed pictogram and one solid-shape fact.

script.say: Quick-fire time! I'll mix everything up — shapes, charts, symmetry. Every right answer grows your streak. Remember the champion rules: key first, hidden parts too. Ready… go!
script.adaptHints: Announce the streak after each correct answer ('that's three in a row!'). Use the child's interests for chart categories — never change the numbers.

stuckProtocol: Name why: which concept slipped — the key, the hidden faces, or the 2-D/3-D words?
Show the matching picture (the pictogram with its key, or the cube drawing) and look at it together.
One hint: 'Key first — what is ONE symbol worth?' or 'Turn the solid in your mind.'
Re-ask an easier version (smaller key, simpler shape), then build back up.
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — the streak can restart, that's how champions train.'

plan.goal: Honest self-assessment: which Unit 7 question felt easiest, which needs more practice; end on a win.
plan.note: Child-led reflection. Log the named weak spot — it becomes the next lesson's warm-up.
plan.successCriteria: Child names one strong area and one to practise, honestly.

script.say: What a round! Tell me — which question felt easiest today, and which one would you like more practice on? … That's really honest, and knowing your tricky spot is a champion move. You read the key before every chart question — that habit stuck. Brilliant.
script.adaptHints: Praise the specific process observed this session (key first, counting hidden faces, checking before answering). Record the named weak spot for the Unit 8 warm-ups.

block.prompt: How many sides does a triangle have?
block.explain: Tri- means three — a triangle has 3 straight sides.

wrongAnswers.why: confused with a square
wrongAnswers.remedy: Trace a triangle in the air with your finger — count each straight line as you draw it.

wrongAnswers.why: confused with a pentagon
wrongAnswers.remedy: TRIangle — like a TRIcycle with 3 wheels. Draw it and count.

hints: 'Tri' means three, like a tricycle.
Draw one in the air and count the lines.

reteach.say: Let's draw it together: one line across, one line up to a point, one line back down. Three lines, three sides — that's why it's a TRI-angle.

block.prompt: In a tally chart, how do we show the number 5?
options: Four strokes with a fifth crossing them
block.explain: Tallies bundle into gates of 5 — four standing strokes and the fifth lying across, so counting in 5s is easy.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: Four strokes with a fifth crossing them (a gate of 5)

wrongAnswers.why: forgot the crossing stroke that closes the gate
wrongAnswers.remedy: Five loose strokes are hard to count fast. What does the fifth stroke DO to the four?

wrongAnswers.why: mixed up tallying with writing numerals
wrongAnswers.remedy: Tallies are little sticks we draw one at a time as we count. How does the fifth stick go?

hints: Think of a gate — four posts and one bar across.
The fifth stroke lies down across the other four.

reteach.say: Watch me tally to five: stick, stick, stick, stick — and the fifth stick lies ACROSS them like a gate closing. Now the bundle shouts 'FIVE!' at a glance, and we can count charts in 5s: 5, 10, 15…

block.caption: Four strokes + one across = a gate of 5

practiceBank.skill: read a pictogram with a key

block.prompt: Pictogram key: 1 🍎 = 5. A row shows 4 apples. How many apples were picked?

wrongAnswers.why: ignored the key and counted each symbol as 1
wrongAnswers.remedy: Key first! What is ONE apple picture worth? Now count in 5s along the row.

wrongAnswers.why: added the key to the count (5 + 4)
wrongAnswers.remedy: The key isn't added — EVERY picture is worth 5. Count: 5, 10, 15…

hints: Read the key first — one picture is worth 5.
Count in 5s: 5, 10, 15, …

reteach.say: The key is the secret code: one apple picture means FIVE real apples. Four pictures — touch each one and count in 5s: 5, 10, 15, 20. Twenty apples!

block.prompt: How many faces does a cube have?
block.explain: Turn the cube in your mind: top, bottom, front, back, left, right — 6 faces, even the hidden ones count.

wrongAnswers.why: counted only the faces you can see at once
wrongAnswers.remedy: Spin the cube in your mind — what's hiding at the back, the bottom, the other side?

wrongAnswers.why: counted vertices instead of faces
wrongAnswers.remedy: Faces are the FLAT surfaces, like the sides of a dice. Count the flats: top, bottom…

hints: Think of a dice — it has a number on every face.
Top and bottom, front and back, left and right — pairs!

reteach.say: A cube is like a dice. A dice shows numbers 1 to 6 — one number per face. So a cube must have exactly 6 faces, even though you can only ever SEE three at once. The hidden ones still count!

block.caption: A dice has faces 1–6 → a cube has 6 faces

block.prompt: A block diagram shows dogs = 6 and cats = 4. How many MORE dogs than cats?

wrongAnswers.why: added the two bars instead of finding the difference
wrongAnswers.remedy: 'How many MORE' is a comparing question — find the gap between the bars, don't join them.

wrongAnswers.why: just read the taller bar
wrongAnswers.remedy: 6 is how many dogs. The question asks how many EXTRA dogs — count up from 4 to 6.

hints: 'How many more' means find the difference.
Count up from 4 to 6 — how many steps?

reteach.say: Picture the two bars standing side by side. The cat bar reaches 4; the dog bar reaches 6. The dog bar pokes ABOVE the cat bar by the gap: 5, 6 — two steps. Two more dogs than cats.

block.statement: A square has a line of symmetry.
block.explain: Fold a square in half — the halves match exactly. In fact a square has 4 lines of symmetry.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: True — a square has 4 lines of symmetry

wrongAnswers.why: unsure what a line of symmetry is, or thinks only 'fancy' shapes have them
wrongAnswers.remedy: Imagine folding a square down the middle. Do the two halves land exactly on top of each other?

hints: Imagine folding it — do the halves match?
Try folding top-to-bottom, side-to-side, and corner-to-corner.

reteach.say: The fold test never lies: fold a square top to bottom — the halves match. Side to side — match. Corner to corner both ways — match, match! Four perfect folds, four lines of symmetry.

block.caption: Fold a square 4 ways — the halves always match

wrongAnswers.why: confused hexagon with pentagon
wrongAnswers.remedy: Pentagon is 5, HEXagon is one more. Trace and count its sides.

wrongAnswers.why: confused hexagon with octagon
wrongAnswers.remedy: An octagon is the stop-sign shape with 8. A hexagon is like a honeycomb cell — count its sides.

hints: Think of a honeycomb cell.
It's one more side than a pentagon.

reteach.say: Bees know this one! Every cell in a honeycomb is a hexagon — count around one: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Six sides, six vertices.

block.caption: Hexagon = 6 sides, like a honeycomb cell

block.prompt: How many vertices does a rectangle have?
block.explain: A rectangle has 4 corners — 4 vertices — and 4 sides.

wrongAnswers.why: counted only the long sides or two corners
wrongAnswers.remedy: Vertices are the corners. Touch every corner of a book cover and count.

wrongAnswers.why: guessing / mixing shapes up
wrongAnswers.remedy: Picture a door or a book — go round it corner by corner: 1, 2, 3, 4.

hints: Vertices are the corners.
Picture a book cover — touch each corner.

reteach.say: Grab an imaginary book. Touch the corners one at a time: top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left. Four corners — four vertices. And four sides joining them.

block.prompt: Sort these words into the right family.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: side, line of symmetry → 2-D; face, edge → 3-D

wrongAnswers.why: uses 'face' for flat shapes in everyday talk
wrongAnswers.remedy: In maths a FACE is a flat surface OF A SOLID — a dice has 6 of them. What do we call the straight lines of a flat shape?

wrongAnswers.why: everyday 'side of the box' language
wrongAnswers.remedy: For solids we say faces and edges. SIDES belong to flat shapes like triangles and pentagons.

hints: Faces and edges belong to solids you can hold.
Sides belong to flat shapes you can draw.

reteach.say: Two word families. Flat shapes — the ones we DRAW — have sides, vertices and lines of symmetry. Solid shapes — the ones we HOLD, like a dice — have faces, edges and vertices. Vertices is the sneaky word that lives in both families!

block.caption: Which words belong to which shapes

practiceBank.skill: read a pictogram with a key

block.prompt: Stretch! Key: 1 ⚽ = 2. A row shows 3 whole footballs and one HALF football. How many goals is that?

wrongAnswers.why: counted the half symbol as a whole one
wrongAnswers.remedy: The half picture is only worth HALF the key. If a whole ball is 2, half a ball is…?

wrongAnswers.why: ignored the key (counted symbols as 1 each) and dropped the half
wrongAnswers.remedy: Key first! One ball = 2 goals. Count in 2s, then add the half-ball's share.

hints: Whole balls first: 2, 4, 6.
Half a ball is worth half of 2.

reteach.say: Count the whole balls in 2s: 2, 4, 6. Now the half ball — a whole ball means 2, so half a ball means just 1. Six and one more: seven goals. Half the symbol, half the value!

block.prompt: A friend draws a line straight through the middle of a shape and says 'that's ALWAYS a line of symmetry'. Are they right? How would you check?
block.sample: No — a line is only a line of symmetry if folding along it makes the two halves match exactly. You check by folding (or imagining the fold).

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: No — only if folding makes both halves match exactly; test with the fold test

wrongAnswers.why: the 'any line' misconception — hasn't tested with folding
wrongAnswers.remedy: Picture a scalene triangle (all sides different). Fold it anywhere — do the halves ever match? So does every middle line work?

wrongAnswers.answer: You check by measuring the sides
wrongAnswers.why: right instinct to check, wrong test
wrongAnswers.remedy: The real test is the FOLD: fold on the line — do the halves land exactly on top of each other?

hints: What's the fold test?
Think of a shape where the halves DON'T match when you fold.

reteach.say: A line of symmetry has to pass the fold test: fold on the line, and both halves must land EXACTLY on top of each other — no bits poking out. Lots of middle lines fail the test. Some shapes, like a scalene triangle, have no line of symmetry at all!

block.caption: Fold test: butterfly halves match; a boot's don't

adaptivity.levelUp: 2 consecutive correct at the current level → next level; at level 3, keep interleaving (never two items of the same skill in a row) and ask 'explain why' on one answer.
adaptivity.levelDown: 2 misses on the same skill → run that item's reteach with the picture in view, then serve a level-1 item of the same skill.
adaptivity.masterySignal: 5+ correct across mixed skills at levels 2–3, including a keyed pictogram read (key first) and a solid-shape fact (hidden faces) → Unit 7 retrieval secure, mastery ≥ 0.8 for shape, data and symmetry.
struggleProtocol: Name why — which concept slipped (the key, hidden faces, 2-D/3-D words, the fold test).
Bring the matching picture back on screen and look at it together.
Give ONE hint ('key first' / 'turn it in your mind' / 'fold it in your head').
Re-ask an easier version (smaller key, simpler shape), then build back up.
Keep it safe: 'The streak can restart — that's how champions train.'
adaptivity.personalization: Use the learner's interests for chart categories and quiz framing (their favourite animals, teams, collections) — never change the numbers or the shape facts.
adaptivity.endOnSuccess: Finish on a question from the child's strongest skill so the streak ends on a win; give specific process praise ('you read the key first every single time').

differentiation.support: Keep the shape picture or chart on screen while answering; fewer, slower questions; whisper 'corners' for vertices.
differentiation.stretch: Explain WHY each answer is right; a timed no-look streak; the half-symbol pictogram item.

extension: Be the quiz master — the child invents three Unit 7 questions (with answers) and fires them at the tutor, who deliberately gets one wrong for the child to correct.
assessmentEvidence: Child fluently recalls 2-D and 3-D shape properties, reads a keyed pictogram and a block diagram correctly, and applies the fold test for symmetry.
revisitLater: Use the child's named weak spot as the warm-up for Lesson 26; fold shape/data questions into the Lesson 28 champion circuit.
